## Parameter Estimation for Supervised Learning

Let us now step back to the world of **supervised learning**,  
where (in the general stochastic case) we have a **training set**:

$$
S = \{(x^{(1)}, y^{(1)}), (x^{(2)}, y^{(2)}), \dots, (x^{(m)}, y^{(m)})\}
$$

**Samples are drawn from a distribution**:

$$
D(X, Y) = D(X) D(Y | X)
$$

where:
- $X$ is the set of **input features**.
- $Y$ is the set of **target responses**.
  - $Y$ can be a **finite set of classes** (for **classification**)  
  - or a **real line** $\mathbb{R}$ (for **regression**).

By **Bayes’ Rule**, we can split our true distributions:

$$
D(X, Y) = D(X) D(Y | X)
$$

where:
- $D(X)$ is the **marginal distribution**.
- $D(Y | X)$ is the **conditional distribution**.


### Probabilistic Models in Supervised Learning

In the **supervised ML** setting, we want our **learning algorithm $A$**  
to find a **hypothesis** $h$ which, given an unseen example $x \in X$,  
is able to predict a **probability distribution** over the target space $Y$:

$$
h(x) = P(Y | X = x)
$$

(This is called a **Probabilistic Model**.)


### Classification vs. Regression

#### **Classification**  
For **classification**, $P(Y | X = x)$ is a **probability mass function (pmf)**.

- We output the **class**:

  $$
  y^* = \arg\max_{y \in Y} P(Y = y | X = x)
  $$

  (i.e., the **most probable** class).

#### **Regression**  
For **regression**, $P(Y | X = x)$ is a **probability density function (pdf)**.

- We output the **mean (expected) value** of this distribution:

  $$
  y^* = \mathbb{E}[Y | X = x]
  $$


### Why Predict a Distribution Instead of a Single Value?

Predicting a **distribution** rather than a single value is more **informative**,  
as it allows us to observe **not just the single predicted value**  
(the one corresponding to the **highest probability**),  
but also informs us of the **uncertainty** and the general distribution **over all target values**.

**Note:**  
In both of the above cases, the probability distribution $P(Y | X = x)$  
is **potentially different for every example** $x \in X$.


We see that we thus want our hypothesis $h_{\Theta}(x)$  
to **output a probability distribution** $P(Y | X = x)$.  

We notice that this probability distribution **might be different**  
for each $x \in X$, and that $X$ is an **infinite space**,  
thus we might have an **infinite number of probability distributions**.  

As we shall see, different learning algorithms handle this differently,  
while maintaining a **finite number of parameters**.


### Discriminative vs. Generative Modeling

Now, given the goal that we want our learning algorithm $A$  
to output a **hypothesis** $h_{\Theta}(x)$ such that:

$$
h_{\Theta}(x) = P(Y | X = x)
$$

there are **two ways** in which the hypothesis can be **set up**  
to output such a probability distribution:  

1. **Discriminative Modeling**  
2. **Generative Modeling**


### **(i) Discriminative Modeling**

Here, our **hypothesis is an estimate of the conditional distribution** $P(Y | X)$.

- Typically, we assume that this **distribution has a certain shape**  
  and fix the hypothesis function to be the **corresponding parameterized probability function**  
  (with parameter set $\Theta$).

- Thus, the **output probability distribution** is:

$$
h_{\Theta}(x) = P(Y | X = x, \Theta)
$$


### **(ii) Generative Modeling**

Here, our **hypothesis is an estimate of the full joint distribution** $P(X, Y)$.

- Typically, we assume that this **distribution has a certain shape**  
  and fix the hypothesis function to be the **corresponding parameterized probability function**  
  (with parameter set $\Theta$).

- The **output probability distribution** is:

$$
h_{\Theta}(x) = \frac{P(X = x, Y | \Theta)}{P(X = x | \Theta)}
$$

where we **calculate the value** of the **marginal probability** $P(X)$  
using the **law of total probability**:

$$
P(X = x) = \sum_{y} P(X = x, Y = y | \Theta) \quad \text{(if $Y$ is discrete)}
$$

$$
P(X = x) = \int P(X = x, Y = y | \Theta) \, dy \quad \text{(if $Y$ is continuous)}
$$


## Generative vs. Discriminative Models

| **Generative** | **Discriminative** |
|---------------|------------------|
|               |                  |


In our **setup**, both **generative** & **discriminative** hypotheses  
are assumed to have **parameters** $\Theta$,  
which determine the exact shape of the distribution $P(Y | X, \Theta)$.  

Said another way, they are **parametric probabilistic hypotheses/models**.


### Model Selection in Supervised Learning

Now, we arrive at the **same question** as in **density estimation**:  

> How should our learning algorithm $A: S \to H$  
> (which is **deterministic**)  
> select the **best set of parameters** $\Theta \in H$?  

Surprisingly, the **answer is the same**!  

Depending on the problem (**classification**/**regression**),  
both **generative & discriminative hypotheses** can be found using  
the **MAP & MLE rules**.


Concretely, for **supervised learning**,  
we select the **parameters** $\Theta$ which **best explain the data**.


## Maximum a Posteriori Estimation (MAP)

The **parameters which best explain the data**  
are the ones with the **highest probability**  
under the observed **supervised training set**:

$$
S = \{(x^{(1)}, y^{(1)}), (x^{(2)}, y^{(2)}), \dots, (x^{(m)}, y^{(m)})\}
$$

For convenience, we will represent **$S$ separately** as:

$$
S_x = \{x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \dots, x^{(m)}\}, \quad S_y = \{y^{(1)}, y^{(2)}, \dots, y^{(m)}\}
$$

where $S = (S_x, S_y)$.

Thus, our **MAP rule** will pick **parameters**  
with the **highest probability**, given $S_x, S_y$:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(\Theta | S_x, S_y)
$$

Using **Bayes’ Rule**, we can express this as:

$$
P(\Theta | S_x, S_y) = \frac{P(S_x, S_y | \Theta) P(\Theta)}{P(S_x, S_y)}
$$

where:

$$
P(S_x, S_y | \Theta)
$$

is called the **likelihood of the observed data given the parameters** $\Theta$.  

Some texts denote this as:

$$
L(\Theta | S_x, S_y) = P(S_x, S_y | \Theta)
$$

but we will use $P(S_x, S_y | \Theta)$ for clarity.


### i.i.d. Assumption

Now, $S_x, S_y$ is a **set of** $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ **pairs**,  
where each $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ is assumed to be sampled  
from the **true distribution** $P(X, Y)$ **in an i.i.d. fashion**.  

Thus, they are **independent**:

$$
P(S_x, S_y | \Theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta)
$$


### Optimization Formulation

For the **optimization objective** of **MAP**,  
we can additionally **take the log** of the probabilities:

$$
\log P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta)
$$

(to prevent **underflow**)  
and also **change the maximization objective to a minimization**.


### Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) Formulation of MAP

We can **convert the optimization objective**  
by taking the **negative log**.  

As explained in **density estimation**,  
these two steps **do not change** the optimal $\Theta$.  

Additionally, the **marginal probability** $P(S_x, S_y)$  
can be **ignored** for a maximization/minimization.

Thus:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(\Theta | S_x, S_y) = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(S_x, S_y | \Theta) P(\Theta)
$$

Using the **i.i.d. assumption** and the **Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) formulation**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} - \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta) - \log P(\Theta)
$$

This gives the **Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL)** form.


## Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

As explained in **density estimation**,  
if we have no reason to **prefer** one set of parameters over another,  
we can **set the prior** to be **uniform**,  
i.e., $P(\Theta) = \frac{1}{|H|}$.

Thus, the **optimization objective**  
becomes to **minimize the Negative Log-Likelihood**,  
which is **equivalent to maximizing** the **likelihood probability distribution**.  

We thus call this the **Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) procedure**.

$$
\Theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} P(S_x, S_y | \Theta)
$$

Applying the **Negative Log-Likelihood**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} - \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta)
$$


### Observations:

1. **Mathematical Clarity:**
   - The **negative log-likelihood transformation**  
     is correctly formulated.
   - The **MLE as a special case of MAP** (with uniform prior)  
     is clearly stated.

2. **Conceptual Flow:**
   - The transition from **MAP to MLE** is well-motivated.
   - The importance of **NLL for optimization stability** is highlighted.

3. **Possible Refinements:**
   - The phrase **"if we have no reason to prefer one set of parameters over another"**  
     could explicitly mention **non-informative priors**.
   - An **example with a Gaussian likelihood**  
     could demonstrate **MLE in action**.

for a **Gaussian distribution** (estimating $\mu, \sigma$)?


For both **MAP & MLE** in the **supervised setting**  
(where we wish to estimate the **joint distribution** $P(X, Y)$),  
we see that there is a **term** $P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}, \Theta)$,  
which comes from applying the **i.i.d. assumption**  
for the **likelihood factor** in **Bayes’ Rule**:

$$
P(S_x, S_y | \Theta)
$$


### **Discriminative vs. Generative Models**

Both **discriminative** & **generative** models  
need **some way** to create a probability distribution $P(X, Y | \Theta)$.  

- **Discriminative models** substitute $P(X, Y | \Theta)$  
  with $P(Y | X, \Theta)$ to obtain a **probability value**:

  $$
  P(Y = y | X = x, \Theta)
  $$

- **Generative models** attempt to estimate  
  the **joint probability distribution** $P(X, Y | \Theta)$.

  - When we need to **predict**, we use:

    $$
    h_{\Theta}(x) = P(Y | X = x, \Theta) = \frac{P(X = x, Y | \Theta)}{P(X = x | \Theta)}
    $$

    - $P(Y | X = x, \Theta)$ → **probability distribution**
    - $P(X = x | \Theta)$ → **probability value**

  - We calculate $P(X | \Theta)$ as:

    $$
    P(X | \Theta) = \sum_{y} P(X, Y = y | \Theta)
    $$

    Thus, **generative models** **indirectly estimate** $P(Y | X, \Theta)$  
    **by way of** $P(X | \Theta)$.


### **Discriminative Models**

On the other hand, we see that **discriminative models**  
directly estimate:

$$
P(Y | X, \Theta)
$$

where:

$$
P(X | \Theta) = P(Y | X, \Theta) P(X | \Theta)
$$

For **discriminative models**, the parameters $\Theta$  
do **not affect** the **marginal distribution** $P(X | \Theta) = P(X)$,  
and only output the **conditional distribution** $P(Y | X, \Theta)$.


### **MAP Estimation for Discriminative Models**

For **discriminative models**, MAP is formulated as:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(\Theta | S_x, S_y)
$$

Using **Bayes’ Rule**:

$$
= \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(\Theta) P(S_y | S_x, \Theta) P(X = S_x | \Theta)
$$

Since for **discriminative models**,  
$P(X | \Theta) = P(X)$ is **constant**, we simplify:

$$
= \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(\Theta) P(S_y | S_x, \Theta)
$$

Applying the **i.i.d. assumption**:

$$
= \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} P(\Theta) \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}, \Theta)
$$


### For Discriminative Models: (where we estimate $P(Y | X, \Theta)$)

Using the **i.i.d. assumption**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} \left[ P(\Theta) \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}, \Theta) \right]
$$

Applying the **Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) formulation**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} \left[ P(\Theta) - \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}, \Theta) \right]
$$

→ **NLL form**


For **MLE**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}, \Theta)
$$

Applying **NLL transformation**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} \sum_{i=1}^{m} -\log P(y^{(i)} | x^{(i)}, \Theta)
$$

→ **NLL form**


### For Generative Models: (where we estimate $P(X, Y | \Theta)$)

Using the **i.i.d. assumption**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} \left[ P(\Theta) \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta) \right]
$$

Applying **NLL transformation**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} \left[ P(\Theta) - \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta) \right]
$$



For **MLE**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_{\Theta \in H} \prod_{i=1}^{m} P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta)
$$

Applying **NLL transformation**:

$$
\Theta_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\min_{\Theta \in H} \sum_{i=1}^{m} -\log P(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} | \Theta)
$$
